content: The need for a comprehensive evaluation of noise-related annoyance was highlighted in the proceedings of the 6th International Congress on Noise as a Public Health Problem, held in Nice, France, from July 5 to 9, 1993. This event was organized by the Institut National de Recherche sur les Transports et leur Sécurité in Lyon. Vogel et al. (2011) investigated the risky listening behaviors of adolescents using MP3 players and their psychosocial correlates, publishing their findings in Health Education Research (Volume 26, Issue 2, Pages 254–264). In a subsequent study, Vogel et al. (2014) explored the association between risky music listening habits, permanent tinnitus, depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and general health outcomes. This research was published in PloS One (Volume 9, Issue 6, Article e98912). Weichbold and Zorowka (2003) examined the impact of a hearing protection campaign on the disco attendance habits of high school students, with their findings appearing in the International Journal of Audiology (Volume 42, Issue 8, Pages 489–493). In 2007, the same authors assessed whether a hearing education campaign could alter adolescents' music listening behaviors, publishing their results in the International Journal of Audiology (Volume 46, Issue 3, Pages 128–133). The World Health Organization (WHO) Constitution, adopted in 1946 and effective from April 7, 1948, defines health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. WHO has since developed numerous guidelines addressing public health concerns, including community noise (1999), air quality (2006), and the global burden of disease (2013). These guidelines are accessible through WHO's official website. In 2014, WHO introduced metrics such as Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) to quantify the burden of disease. The same year, WHO published a report on the health impacts of ambient air pollution in 2012 and released a second edition of its handbook for guideline development. In 2015, WHO reviewed the effects of recreational exposure to loud sounds on hearing loss. The WHO Regional Office for Europe has also contributed significantly to environmental health research. In 2009, it published night noise guidelines for Europe, followed by the Parma Declaration on Environment and Health in 2010. In 2012, it assessed the need for capacity-building in health risk assessment for environmental noise. In 2016, it released principles for assessing health risks associated with air pollution, and in 2017, it provided databases for data and evidence on environmental health. The burden of disease from environmental noise in Europe was quantified in a 2011 report by the WHO Regional Office for Europe and the Joint Research Centre (JRC). This report estimated the loss of healthy life years due to noise exposure. Research by Wiens (1995) in Berlin (West) examined the relationship between transportation noise and cardiovascular risk, while Wilson and Lonigan (2010) evaluated tools for identifying preschool children at risk of future reading difficulties. Yano et al. (2005) conducted a survey on community responses to Shinkansen noise and vibration along the Sanyo Shinkansen Line. Similarly, Morinaga et al. (2015) studied community reactions to changes in aircraft noise exposure near Noi Bai Airport in Hanoi. Yokoshima et al. (2008) reanalyzed response curves for Shinkansen railway noise, and Yoshida et al. (1997) investigated the effects of road traffic noise on Tokyo residents. The WHO Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region were developed with input from various experts and organizations. These guidelines address critical health outcomes such as cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, cognitive impairment, mental health, sleep disturbance, adverse birth outcomes, hearing impairment, and annoyance. The guidelines also provide recommendations for noise interventions and implementation strategies. Systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the evidence on environmental noise and its health impacts. For example, Basner and McGuire (2018) reviewed the effects of noise on sleep, while Brown and van Kamp (2017) examined the impact of transport noise interventions on health. Clark and Paunovic (2018) reviewed the effects of noise on cognition, quality of life, and mental health. Guski et al. (2017) focused on noise annoyance, and Śliwińska-Kowalska and Zaborowski (2017) investigated permanent hearing loss and tinnitus. Nieuwenhuijsen et al. (2017) reviewed adverse birth outcomes, and van Kempen et al. (2018) summarized cardiovascular and metabolic effects. The guideline development process included conflict of interest management. All contributors, including members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), Systematic Review Team, and External Review Group, submitted declarations of interest. These declarations were reviewed by WHO technical staff to ensure transparency and minimize bias. No contributors were excluded from the process due to conflicts of interest. The evidence retrieval process categorized health outcomes as either critical or important for decision-making. Systematic reviews were conducted for both categories, with critical outcomes informing the recommendations. Important outcomes, such as adverse birth outcomes, quality of life, mental health, and metabolic effects, were also reviewed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the health impacts of environmental noise. This version maintains the detailed content while presenting it in a clear, professional, and accessible manner.
